sources.citation: Ray, Sidney H. 1926. A Comparative Study of the Melanesian Island Languages. Cambridge: CUP. 'Grammar of the Utupua Language', pp. 461-469 (= Asumboa [aua], from a MS by Rev. B. Teilo).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request); access check: open copy online; also held in print at Harvard (Widener Library (offsite storage), call number 2234.7.25)
sources.note: Describes Asumboa, not Amba (Glottolog assigns it to aua). Its 'Alphabet' and 'Sounds' sections have no accent/stress statement (per the sibling check's scanned).

Nothing on phonology beyond the endonym [aᵐba] with prenasalised [ᵐb] and the Asumboa exonym [neᵐbao]; sole bibliography item is Tryon 1994. The Temotu page cites Ross & Næss 2007, Lackey & Boerger 2021, François 2009, Blench 2014.

sources.citation: Ross, Malcolm & Åshild Næss. 2007. An Oceanic origin for Äiwoo, the language of the Reef Islands? Oceanic Linguistics 46(2): 456-498.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Comparative-historical paper that establishes the Temotu subgroup with Utupua data (from Tryon); may contain phonological remarks on Utupua languages including prosody; Unpaywall reports closed access.

sources.citation: Ethnologue entries for Amba [utp]: Gordon (ed.) 2005, Ethnologue 15th ed. web report 'AMBA: a language of Solomon Islands' (14th-ed. data, Internet Archive copy 2005-02-26) and Lewis, Simons & Fennig (eds) 2014, Ethnologue 17th ed. 'Amba' (Internet Archive copy 2015-02-16).
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: 14th/15th ed.: 'Comments: Bilingualism in Pijin. SVO. Literacy rate in first language: 10% to 30%..'; 17th ed.: 'Typology: SVO.' No stress, syllable-type or tone field in either edition.

sources.citation: Lynch, John, Malcolm Ross & Terry Crowley. 2002. The Oceanic Languages. Richmond: Curzon. Sect. 5.2 'Utupua and Vanikoro'; Tryon's Buma (Vanikoro) sketch sect. 1.3 Stress.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on Amba/Utupua stress; Utupua is mentioned only for subgrouping. The Buma (Vanikoro) sketch says 'Stress normally occurs on the penultimate syllable except if the final syllable contains a long vowel, in which case the final syllable is stressed' - a different island and family, not applicable to Amba.

sources.citation: Dutton, Tom & Darrell T. Tryon (eds). 1994. Language contact and change in the Austronesian world (Trends in Linguistics. Studies and Monographs 77). Berlin/New York: Mouton de Gruyter. ISBN 3-11-012786-5. [Held sidecar is the text of the whole 696-page volume although catalogued under Rivierre's chapter 'Contact-induced phonological complexification in New Caledonia', pp. 497-522, DOI 10.1515/9783110883091.497; chapters read for targets: Adelaar 'The classification of the Tamanic languages' 1-42; Bugenhagen 'Language change on Umboi Island' 43-108; Clark 'The Polynesian Outliers as a locus of language contact' 109-139; Dutton 'Motu-Koiarian contact in Papua New Guinea' 181-232; B. D. Grimes 'Cloves and nutmeg..' 251-274; Reid 'Unravelling the linguistic histories of Philippine Negritos' 443-475; Tryon 'Language contact and contact-induced language change in the Eastern Outer Islands, Solomon Islands' 611-648; Voorhoeve '..north Moluccas' 649-674.]
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No statement on stress or tone: Tryon's sketch is morphosyntactic (possessive classes, pronouns, TAM marking) plus loanword lists and a POC consonant-reflex table; no phoneme inventory or prosody section for Nembao.

sources.citation: Tryon, Darrell T. & B. D. Hackman. 1983. Solomon Islands Languages: An Internal Classification (Pacific Linguistics C-72). Canberra: ANU. Nembao (Amba) = wordlist no. 99, Utupua; Utupua/Vanikoro sound-correspondence tables and subgrouping discussion.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent on Nembao/Amba stress. Nembao appears in the language census (150 speakers), the name index (Aba, Amba, Aruba = NEMBAO) and the comparative reflex tables (e.g. POC *niuR > Nembao nie); the only 'stress' tokens in the file are footnotes 'in unstressed position' on vowel reflexes, not a placement statement.

sources.citation: Tryon, D. T. 1982. Towards a classification of Solomon Islands languages. In Amran Halim, Lois Carrington & S. A. Wurm (eds), Papers from the Third International Conference on Austronesian Linguistics, vol. 1: Currents in Oceanic, 97-108. Pacific Linguistics C-74. Canberra: ANU.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Classification lists only; the words stress/accent/tone do not occur in the paper.

sources.citation: Grace, George W. 1955-1956. Field notebooks and TRIPP reports, 'The George Grace linguistic research and slides of Melanesia collection, 1955-1956', University of Hawai'i at Manoa Library Digital Collections (items 01-52; language inventory by Grace, 2007, item 08 = media/).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: not downloaded: zero-download mode (the three Nembao notebooks themselves); inventory read held by the project confirms coverage. Handwritten 1955 phonetic wordlists/pronoun notes; Grace's other Solomons pages carry occasional phonetic remarks and stress ticks but no stated rules, so at best 'marks only' is expected.

sources.citation: Lackey, William James & Brenda H. Boerger. 2021. Reexamining the phonological history of Oceanic's Temotu subgroup. Oceanic Linguistics 60(2): 367-411.
